title: Redwood Migration Demo - OpenAI/Anthropic/Together parity mapping
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-26 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 min | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Ramesh (Redwood) - Daniel Park, Maya Lopez, Ravi Singh (NovaQuant)

Summary: quick migration/demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together APIs to Redwood's API and Console. Covered API param mapping, streaming and function-calling differences, embeddings name mapping, performance/latency tradeoffs, and security implications (VPC/private, KMS, SOC2). Agreed next steps: share parity spreadsheet, run a small benchmark, and schedule POC kickoff.

Topics: API parity, function calling mapping, embeddings parity, streaming behavior, batching & optimize recommendations, security/compliance, pricing estimate, POC scope

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex with Redwood, AE. Quick intro - Priya our SE will run the demo and I'll cover pricing/next steps.
[00:12] Daniel: Thanks Alex. I'm Daniel, CTO at NovaQuant. We brought Maya and Ravi - Maya handles model infra, Ravi SRE. We're evaluating moving away from OpenAI/Together toward something more cost predictable and deployable in our VPC.
[00:24] Priya: Awesome, yeah we'll focus on the parity mapping - basically how your existing OpenAI/Anthropic/Together calls translate to Redwood API and Console, and highlight gaps.
[00:38] Maya: Two high level items - 1) function calling: we use OpenAI function calls heavily so how similar is that? 2) embeddings names & vector dimension parity since embeddings tie into our semantic search. Also latency and cost.
[00:52] Priya: Great, we'll show both. Quick note: transcription may chop some tech words, apologies for any mis-hearings - e.g., "KV cache" might be transcribed weird.

--- Demo start ---
[02:10] Priya: Opening the Redwood Console - top nav has Models, Endpoints, Optimize. Here is a sample API parity doc we keep in the workspace. On the left you can map OpenAI params: "model", "temperature", "max_tokens", "stop", "stream" to Redwood equivalents. For example model -> model, temperature -> temperature, max_tokens -> max_tokens. Function-calling maps but we call it "tools" in our SDK in some places which can confuse transcripts.
[03:05] Priya: Function calling: Redwood supports a function/tool calling interface compatible with OpenAI-style JSON schema. The difference - in streaming we emit tool invocation events as an intermediate event type. So you can keep similar client-side logic. A small caveat: Together's async tool pattern maps too but requires setting "preserve_kv" param for long conversations.
[03:40] Ravi: Are there any differences in token accounting between OpenAI and Redwood? We bill per-token but our internal cost models rely on counting that exactly.
[03:50] Alex: Good question. Redwood's hosted API uses per-token billing similar to OpenAI; we provide token-level breakdowns in Console and SDK so you can reconcile. There are minor differences around how streaming delimiters/metadata tokens are counted - we document those in the parity spreadsheet we will share.
[04:20] Priya: Now embeddings - we have a mapping table. For example, OpenAI ada-embedding-v2 -> Redwood/embed-2-small (128-dim) as an example; Anthropic embeddings map to equivalent dims. We'll include exact dims and cosine/similarity guidance.
[04:46] Maya: Do you guarantee exact dimension/score parity? We have an existing index and can't re-index everything.
[04:55] Priya: Short answer: not always exact numeric parity across different vendor models, but we provide recommendations and often a 1:1 nearest-match model for dimension-compatible migration to avoid reindexing. If you need bit-exact equivalence that's only possible if same model implementation.

[06:10] Priya: Switching to API demo - here's a sample request that NovaQuant might be running against OpenAI. (screen share) request: POST /v1/chat/completions with model= gpt-4o-sample, messages, functions, stream=true. On Redwood it's similar: POST /v1/responses (we also support a chat-compatible endpoint). Key differences: naming variance (responses vs chat/completions), and we have additional route-level config for batching and caching.
[07:05] Priya: Streaming behavior: Redwood streams tokens with SSE by default and includes occasional system-level events for kv-cache warmup. If you rely on chunked semantics, we provide a drop-in streaming SDK that mirrors OpenAI stream frames.
[07:32] Daniel: Our devs rely on stop sequences and sometimes partial completions to terminate. Any pitfalls?
[07:40] Priya: Stop sequences map 1:1. The main pitfall is when you mix function calls and stops - we emit a function-invocation event and then the tool output. Need to ensure client handles both.

[09:00] Priya: Now the Console - Routes let you pin model versions, add model fallbacks (e.g., if high-cost GPU model congested fallback to quantized variant), and set autoscale/burst. Optimize tab gives quantization suggestions and batching configs per route.
[09:40] Priya: Example Optimize suggestion: for streaming low-latency chat, reduce batch window to 10ms and enable prefix caching on session start; for high-throughput embedding index jobs, run larger batch sizes with asynchronous workers.
[10:12] Maya: How do you handle KV cache for multi-turn chat? We need persistent sessions across shards.
[10:22] Priya: Redwood supports session affinity and persistent KV cache when you enable Dedicated or Private with customer-managed persistence. For hosted customers we keep ephemeral caches but you can use persistent cache add-on. We can also expose cache keys to your infra via the VPC/private model.

[12:00] Ravi: Security - SOC2 and KMS. We need to know whether Redwood can support customer-managed keys and on-prem private control plane.
[12:10] Alex: Yes. Private offers a control plane you run in your VPC, or we can deploy an on-prem bundle for air-gapped environments. KMS/HSM integrations are supported for Private customers; Hosted customers can use customer-managed keys via partner KMS in some regions. SOC2 compliance is in our security pack; we'll share the security whitepaper and SOC2 report.
[12:45] Daniel: Good. Also need SSO, RBAC, audit logs for operator-level changes.
[12:53] Alex: Console has RBAC, SAML SSO integrations, and full audit logging with retention policies. We'll include sample config in the doc pack.

[14:20] Priya: Back to parity - here's a concrete mapping page: OpenAI param -> Redwood param. We also included examples for Anthropic/Together. For example Anthropic's "max_tokens_to_sample" becomes Redwood's "max_tokens"; Together's "safety_level" maps to a content-filter pipeline param in Console.
[15:05] Priya: We try to automate a lot of this in our migration helper script that rewrites calls; it's open-source-ish and we'll link it. It handles model name swaps, param translation, and optional telemetry hooks.

[17:00] Maya: Performance - can you run a quick benchmark for our workload? We're sensitive to p95 latency at ~1800 token responses.
[17:08] Priya: We can. Typical workflow: share a representative prompt set and traffic profile, we run a small benchmark on hosted, Dedicated, and a quantized variant, and produce p50/p95/p99 latency plus cost per 1k tokens. We recommend doing both cold and warmed kv-cache runs.
[17:30] Daniel: How long does that take?
[17:35] Alex: For a 1k prompt set, about 48-72 hours end-to-end to run all variants and aggregate; quick smoke within 24 hours on hosted.

[19:00] Priya: Now I'll demo function-calling flow - (screen) sending messages with functions defined. Here Redwood returns a tool call object, then emits tool output. Client code example in Node and Python. Note: slight schema name differences - e.g., Redwood's call uses "tool" object with name and payload. We show both streaming and non-streaming.
[21:10] Daniel: Maya asked earlier about partial matches in embeddings for semantic search; if dims differ will we get degraded recall?
[21:20] Priya: Yes some drift can occur. Recommendation: use a dimension-compatible Redwood embedding or reindex critical subsets. Our Optimize tab can suggest which models minimize recall regression.

[23:45] Priya: Pricing - quick sketch: hosted per-token pricing, Dedicated monthly commitments, and Private licensing. For migration we usually propose a short POC on hosted first to validate correctness, then Dedicated for scale/cost predictability.
[24:30] Alex: I'll follow up with a preliminary pricing estimate based on your monthly token volume range.

[26:00] Maya: Any migration pitfalls around rate limits and throttling? We have bursty traffic patterns.
[26:10] Priya: You can set per-route throttles and burst configs. Dedicated gives you guaranteed throughput. For hosted we recommend rate limit tiers plus auto-burst to handle spiky loads. We'll add recommended settings based on your peak QPS.

[28:55] Priya: Quick note on observability: Console has token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency heatmaps, and tracing hooks to correlate application traces with token events. We'll show example trace JSON in the doc pack.

[31:10] Ravi: On networking: if we go Private in our AWS account, what's the infra footprint and maintenance overhead?
[31:20] Alex: Private control plane is lightweight; runtime nodes are your responsibility if on-prem, or we deploy managed infra in your VPC. We provide terraform scripts and runbooks. Maintenance windows are configurable and we support enterprise SLAs.

[33:40] Priya: Returning to demo: Console route example with fallback policy - if model A is congested we fallback to quantized model B. That helps reliability without code changes.

[35:12] Daniel: Do you support model rollouts / canary?
[35:17] Priya: Yes - you can specify rollout percentages and auto-rollback on regression signals. We support tying rollouts to eval suites.

[37:05] Maya: Is there an API shim for Together's special tokens/embeddings? We use Together-specific tokens in pre-processing.
[37:14] Priya: We have a preprocessor library that normalizes tokenization differences. Not perfect but helps. We'll include it in the migration repo.

[39:30] Priya: Ok let's talk concrete next steps and POC scope. We propose: 1) share a 500-1k prompt sample and metric targets, 2) Redwood runs hosted smoke and Dedicated estimate, 3) we share parity mapping spreadsheet and migration scripts, 4) schedule POC kickoff.
[40:05] Daniel: Sounds good. Timeline - we want a POC by mid-Jan if possible.
[40:12] Alex: We can do a Jan 10-12 POC kickoff window. We'll confirm by email.

[42:00] Priya: Quick Q&A - Maya: about latency and caching: if you enable prefix caching and persistent kv across Dedicated nodes, p95 improves dramatically for multi-turn. Example numbers we'll include in report.
[42:30] Maya: Great.

[44:00] Alex: We'll also attach a security packet and SOC2 report.

[46:15] Priya: Last demo note: embeddings migration tool will do dimension-checks and suggest model substitutes to minimize reindex. We'll include sample scripts.

[48:00] Daniel: Any competitors we should be aware of in your opinion?
[48:06] Alex: We see direct comparisons vs OpenAI, Anthropic, Together, and inference vendors like Cohere and self-hosted runtime vendors. We'll include competitive positioning in the pack.

[50:20] Priya: Recap: parity mapping doc + migration scripts, run benchmark on representative prompts, share pricing + Dedicated estimate, schedule POC kickoff in early Jan.
[50:40] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security docs by Friday.
[51:00] Daniel: Thanks team, appreciate the walkthrough.
[51:10] Maya: Thanks.
[51:20] Ravi: Thanks, bye.
[51:25] Alex: Bye all.
summary: Demo covering API parity mapping (OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood), function-calling mapping, streaming differences, embeddings mapping, Console features (routes, fallbacks, Optimize), security (Private/VPC, KMS, SOC2), and POC/benchmark plan. Agreed next steps to share parity spreadsheet and run a benchmark.
